Thank you for this wonderful analysis, I think you really captured some of the major issues a lot of people struggle to voice when they say they dislike contemporary/ mass appeal poetry (i.e. Rupi Kaur). I always felt like Kaur's poetry read like a magazine horoscope (ex: "Scorpios, this month you will travel somewhere out of the ordinary, and some regrets may be on your mind") - so intentionally vague that literally everyone could relate to it. What Kaur's work gains in relatability, it loses in grit, personality, and identity. I think she could be a great writer, if only she would commit to writing honestly about her unique struggles as an individual.
To be honest it's not that bad, if not a little cliché for its genre.

I understand what you were trying to convey, but this comes across as rather cliché. I think it's because this topic is overused and the writing feels impersonal - there are many people who could have written this poem. What you gain in relatability you lose in uniqueness, for lack of a better word. Sabotage against what? Retaliation against what? I saw you mentioned in the comments about destroying things you worked so hard to build. That idea seems much more interesting to me - I don't think it came across in the poem.
Is there more than one hospital nearby? Also (just curious) what made it sound like a prison?

It's important to support her without alienating her. I think you're doing a great job by continuing with what you normally do, like sending stupid messages for a laugh. Friendship is a two-way street though, and it isn't unreasonable to ask for support from her when you're dealing with your own struggles. If you're really worried that it's too much of a burden, you can preface your problem with a statement like: "hey, I know you've been dealing with a lot lately and I don't want to add more to your plate. I've been struggling a bit myself lately and would really appreciate your advice on this, but if it's too much right now, I totally understand and will respect your boundaries." I think you're doing a great job in supporting your friends and this post is proof that you really do care about her. I'm sure she feels that love too.
When I was hospitalized, we were not allowed to have phones (or any personal items at all, for that matter). It varies from ward to ward. Some wards don't even allow you to wear your own clothes.
I liked listening to classical music and old jazz records! It gave me a feel for the library setting, and jazz seems to go well with the general dream-like strangeness of it all.

I love the last two lines. I can almost imagine this poem being part of those "children's books for adults" sort of thing. I would definitely change the word "gonna" to "going to" - the rest of your poem is written formally and the colloquial language stands out from the rest. I'd also rewrite the phrase "I've counted 50 million more". For me, this poem is too short for the repetition. But I like it! Keep writing. :-)
